rationale: Systematic cohort evaluations of individuals with FBXO11-related neurodevelopmental disorder confirm that mild-to-moderate microcephaly occurs in approximately 20-25% of assessed individuals (specifically 4 of 19, or 21.1%, in the definitive Gregor et al. 2018 cohort), whereas macrocephaly is documented in a smaller proportion (2 of 19, or 10.5%). Subsequent large-scale clinical series, including Gregor et al. 2022 (23 additional individuals), explicitly reaffirm that while head circumference remains within the normal range for the majority of individuals, microcephaly is consistently more common than macrocephaly. Although isolated familial reports (e.g., Lee et al. 2020) document macrocephaly in specific individuals with truncating variants, such occurrences represent the known minority subset with enlarged head circumference rather than a general skew towards macrocephaly.

evidence.text: In the initial cohort of 20 individuals with de novo FBXO11 variants, head circumference measurements revealed microcephaly in 4 of 19 evaluated individuals (21.1%) and macrocephaly in 2 of 19 evaluated individuals (10.5%), demonstrating that microcephaly is twice as frequent as macrocephaly.

evidence.text: In an expanded study analyzing 23 additional individuals with de novo FBXO11 variants, the authors noted that head circumference was within normal limits for most individuals, and growth parameter analysis showed that microcephaly and short stature were more frequent than macrocephaly and tall stature.

evidence.text: Detailed clinical delineation of two unrelated individuals with de novo FBXO11 loss-of-function variants documented postnatal mild microcephaly or borderline small head circumference in both patients alongside intellectual disability and behavioral problems.

source.quote: Thus, we confirm deleterious de novo mutations in FBXO11 as a cause of ID and start the delineation of the associated clinical picture which may also comprise postnatal microcephaly or borderline small head size and behavioural anomalies.

evidence.text: A familial case of IDDFBA showed autosomal dominant transmission of a heterozygous frameshift duplication (p.Gly803Leufs*6) where the affected mother presented with macrocephaly, confirming that macrocephaly does occur within the FBXO11 phenotypic spectrum, albeit less commonly overall.

new_directions.question_text: Does head circumference standard deviation score correlate with variant type (likely gene-disrupting vs. missense domain-specific alterations) in FBXO11-related disorder?
new_directions.rationale: Initial cohorts hinted that microcephaly may be enriched in individuals with likely gene-disrupting loss-of-function variants, whereas specific missense variants or familial C-terminal frameshifts have exhibited normal or increased head size. Stratifying pooled cohorts by variant location and class will clarify the biological mechanism governing cranial growth.

new_directions.question_text: What is the longitudinal trajectory of head circumference from birth through adulthood in FBXO11 mutation carriers?
new_directions.rationale: Several reports specify that microcephaly is postnatal rather than congenital, suggesting a progressive deceleration of cranial growth that could serve as a valuable distinguishing clinical sign from primary congenital microcephalies.
